title: Integration Patterns, Cost Optimization, KPIs/ROI, and Cloud-First Design
bodyMarkdown:
## Integration patterns and data movement

Decoupling a monolith or connecting systems comes down to a handful of patterns. The Well-Architected [system design principles](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/system-design) say why: decoupled components can be upgraded independently, secured separately and tuned for performance and cost one at a time.

| Pattern | Service | Use for |
|---------|---------|---------|
| Asynchronous messaging and event fan-out | **Pub/Sub** | One event, many consumers; decouple producers from consumers |
| Managed batch and streaming pipelines | **Dataflow** | Code-based ETL at scale with Apache Beam |
| Visual, code-free data integration | **Cloud Data Fusion** | Build pipelines in a web UI without writing code |
| Service orchestration | **Workflows** | Serverless sequencing of HTTP calls and Google Cloud APIs |
| Scheduled, dependency-rich pipelines | **Cloud Composer (now Managed Service for Apache Airflow)** | Python DAGs across clouds and on-premises |
| API exposure | **API Gateway**, **Apigee** | Simple REST façade versus governed API program |
| Change data capture | **Datastream**, **Database Migration Service** | Replicate or migrate operational data |

[Pub/Sub](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/overview) is an asynchronous, scalable messaging service that decouples the services producing messages from those processing them, with typical latencies on the order of 100 milliseconds. Producers publish to a topic and each subscription receives the messages independently, so adding a consumer requires no change to the producer. Subscription types include pull, push, BigQuery, Bigtable and Cloud Storage subscriptions. Delivery is at-least-once, with exactly-once delivery available as an option, so consumers should still be idempotent. It also offers dead-letter queues and filtering. Pub/Sub is the answer to "fan order events out to inventory, analytics and notifications".

[Dataflow](https://cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/overview) provides unified stream and batch processing as a fully managed service built on Apache Beam (Java, Python, Go), with autoscaling, prebuilt templates and exactly-once processing by default; an at-least-once mode exists for cost or latency trade-offs. [Cloud Data Fusion](https://cloud.google.com/data-fusion/docs/concepts/overview) is the visual alternative: a managed integration service powered by open source CDAP that provisions ephemeral Spark clusters to run batch or real-time pipelines and deletes them afterward. Choose Dataflow when engineers want code and streaming control, Data Fusion when analysts or integration teams want a drag-and-drop pipeline.

For orchestration, [Workflows](https://cloud.google.com/workflows/docs/overview) is serverless, charges nothing while idle and combines Cloud Run, Cloud Run functions, Google Cloud APIs and any HTTP API; a workflow can hold state, retry, poll or wait for up to a year. [Managed Service for Apache Airflow](https://cloud.google.com/composer/docs/concepts/overview), which Google's documentation says Cloud Composer is evolving into, is for Airflow DAGs written in Python that coordinate larger scheduled pipelines; it runs Airflow on a GKE cluster with a web server, metadata database and Cloud Storage bucket. Rule of thumb: Workflows for calling services and handling the results; Airflow when you need DAG-based scheduling of larger pipelines and the Airflow ecosystem. You may still see the name Cloud Composer on exam material.

On the API side, [API Gateway](https://cloud.google.com/api-gateway/docs/about-api-gateway) provides managed access to backends (Cloud Run functions, Cloud Run, App Engine standard) through a consistent REST interface defined by OpenAPI 2.0, handling authentication, traffic management and monitoring. [Apigee](https://cloud.google.com/apigee/docs/api-platform/get-started/what-apigee) is the full API management platform: proxies, security policies, analytics, monetization and a developer portal for governed API programs.

Prefer asynchronous, loosely coupled integration for resilience and independent scaling. Synchronous calls are simpler but chain the availability and latency of services together, and the composite availability is the product of the parts.

## Cost optimization

The [cost optimization pillar](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/cost-optimization) has four principles: align cloud spending with business value, foster a culture of cost awareness, optimize resource usage (provision only what you need and pay only for what you consume), and optimize continuously. The meta-rule is *appropriate*, not *cheapest*.

| Lever | Best for | Watch out for |
|-------|----------|---------------|
| **Right-size** | Over-provisioned VMs | [Recommendations](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/apply-machine-type-recommendations-for-instances) use 8 days of metrics, are hidden below $10 per month in savings and unavailable for memory-optimized families and GPU or TPU instances |
| **Spot VMs** | Fault-tolerant, interruptible batch | [Up to 91% discount](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/spot), no SLA, may be unavailable; needs retries and checkpoints |
| **Committed use discounts** | Steady 24/7 baseline | One- or three-year terms, billed monthly whether used or not ([CUD overview](https://cloud.google.com/docs/cuds)) |
| **Scale down when idle** | Variable or periodic load | Cloud Run scales to zero; a MIG reaches zero only with schedule-based autoscaling and minimum replicas 0 |
| **Storage lifecycle** | Aging data | Transitions only move to colder classes; actions are asynchronous |
| **Match resilience to criticality** | DR and HA spend | Tier workloads (Module 2) |

For a nightly, fault-tolerant, retry-friendly pipeline with no tight deadline, the right pair is Spot VMs with idempotent, checkpointed tasks plus workers that scale down between runs. Three-year CUDs sized to peak nightly capacity waste money because nothing runs during the day, and keeping the largest VMs on around the clock is the opposite of the pillar. Spanner multi-region is a resilience feature, not a cost one.

Use [Gemini Cloud Assist](https://cloud.google.com/gemini/docs/cloud-assist/overview) to ask natural-language questions about spending and to analyze cost anomalies, alongside billing and FinOps reporting.

## KPIs and ROI

A good KPI is specific, measurable, time-bound and tied to an outcome. "Better performance" is not a KPI; "reduce p95 checkout latency from 1,200 ms to under 500 ms within 90 days of cutover" is, because it has a metric, baseline, target and deadline. Use the same discipline as SLOs (Module 1).

**ROI** = (benefit - cost) / cost. Benefits include lower TCO, faster time to market, fewer outage losses and better engineering productivity; costs include migration effort, dual-running during cutover, training and licenses. Worked example: a migration costing 400,000 that saves 250,000 a year in infrastructure and avoids 150,000 a year in outage losses returns 400,000 a year, so ROI over one year is (400,000 - 400,000) / 400,000 = 0%, and over three years it is (1,200,000 - 400,000) / 400,000 = 200%. Always state the time horizon. Define KPIs before the project, capture the baseline in the assessment phase, and re-measure afterward so the business case stays honest.

## Cloud-first and future-proofing

- **Prefer managed and serverless services** to reduce toil; buy or repurchase commodity capabilities rather than build them.
- **Design for change.** Containers, infrastructure as code (Terraform), clear service boundaries and stateless components make later replacement cheap.
- **Make trade-offs consciously.** Managed services trade some portability for speed; document the decision and the exit path.
- **Build in observability and automation from day one,** which is the operational excellence pillar.
- **Plan for growth.** Choose data services that scale (Spanner, Bigtable, BigQuery) and global load balancing so 10x growth is a configuration change rather than a rewrite.
- **Run reviews continuously.** Architecture decisions are documented, revisited and re-measured against KPIs.

## Current AI platform naming

Exam content now uses current product names, so recognize them:

| Name | What it is |
|------|-----------|
| **Gemini Cloud Assist** | AI assistance in the console, CLI and IDEs for design, troubleshooting and cost analysis |
| **Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform** | The platform whose documentation under the former Vertex AI paths now uses this name; treat "Vertex AI" as the older name |
| **[Model Garden](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/start/introduction-unified-platform)** | Catalog to explore, test and deploy models from Google and partners |
| **[Model Armor](https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/model-armor-overview)** | Screens LLM prompts and responses for prompt injection and jailbreaks, sensitive data, harmful content and malicious URLs; start in inspect-only mode, then move to inspect-and-block |
| **[AI Hypercomputer](https://cloud.google.com/ai-hypercomputer/docs/overview)** | Integrated supercomputing system: GPUs and TPUs, networking, storage, open software and flexible consumption options such as Spot VMs and reservations |

Use these to place AI workloads during design: safety filtering is Model Armor, model discovery is Model Garden, large-scale training and serving infrastructure is AI Hypercomputer, and cloud operations help is Gemini Cloud Assist.

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **Synchronous chains** between many services, so one slow dependency stalls everything.
- **Polling or point-to-point integrations** where Pub/Sub fan-out would decouple producers and consumers.
- **Wrong orchestrator.** Standing up Airflow for a three-step API sequence, or stretching Workflows to replace a DAG-heavy data platform.
- **Dataflow where a visual tool is requested,** or Data Fusion where streaming control is required.
- **CUDs for variable or peak load,** and Spot for work that cannot be interrupted.
- **Right-sizing only once.** Utilization drifts; the pillar says optimize continuously.
- **Qualitative KPIs** and ROI without a time horizon or baseline.
- **Unexamined lock-in avoidance,** such as building a portability layer for a service you will never move, which adds cost without value.
- **Treating cheapest as best,** which sacrifices an NFR you were required to meet.

## Exam tips

- **Pub/Sub for fan-out, Dataflow or Data Fusion for pipelines.** One event to many independent consumers is Pub/Sub; managed ETL is Dataflow (code) or Data Fusion (visual); Interconnect, CDN and snapshots do not do messaging or ETL.
- **Batch plus fault-tolerant plus flexible deadline means Spot and scale-down,** not long-term commitments sized to peak or always-on large VMs.
- **CUDs are for steady baseline load;** you pay the commitment whether you use it or not.
- **A proper KPI has a metric, baseline, target and date.** ROI is (benefit - cost) / cost over a stated horizon.
- **Workflows for service orchestration, Airflow (formerly Cloud Composer) for DAG-based pipelines;** API Gateway for a simple REST front, Apigee for governed API management.
- **Prefer managed, serverless, decoupled, stateless designs** and document the trade-offs; cloud-first does not mean cheapest or most portable.
- **Match the AI product to the job:** Gemini Cloud Assist for console help, Model Garden for models, Model Armor for prompt and response screening, AI Hypercomputer for AI infrastructure.
- **Cost optimization means appropriate spend.** Match resilience, capacity and discount commitments to the actual requirement.
